generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, reflection is built into how you learn across every subject, from sport and exercise science to coaching, management and rehabilitation. After a lab session, a coaching practical, or a placement, you are expected to look back and ask not just what you found but how you worked. Sport science students weigh lab data and testing, coaching students weigh what they saw in a session, management students weigh participation evidence. The methods differ, yet the honest look-back is shared. A School of Sport degree treats that look-back as part of becoming a competent, self-aware practitioner, not an optional extra.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students who have just had the same physiology lab report returned with a middling mark and some feedback.

Tom reads the feedback, notes that the mark was lower than hoped, and writes: 'I got 56. The marker said my analysis of the VO2 max data was thin and my results reporting was off. I will try harder next time.' This records what happened and ends with a vague intention. It is a description, not a reflection: it never asks why the analysis was thin or what 'trying harder' would actually involve.

Amara reads the same feedback and looks back honestly. 'My analysis was thin because I reported the VO2 max values but never linked them to the training status of the participants or the wider literature. The results reporting slipped because I rushed the tables at the end. Next time I will build the analysis around each physiological measure, and format the data as I write it up.' This is reflection: it asks why things went as they did and turns that into specific, doable changes.

Both students looked back at the same report. Only Amara moved past describing it to learning from it.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, reflection is a deliberate, honest look back at your work, whether a lab report, a coaching practical, or a placement, so that you can learn from it rather than simply describe what happened. You can now explain what reflection is, recognise it in how a student looks back on their work, and say why it matters: it is how a self-regulating sport practitioner turns experience into improvement. The next lesson gives you a simple model for doing it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's log a reflection rather than a description?

items.text: She asked why her analysis and results reporting fell short, and turned it into specific changes.
She recorded her mark and the marker's comments accurately.
She wrote more than Tom did.
She promised to try harder next time.

feedback.correct: That's right. Asking why things fell short and planning specific changes is what makes it a reflection.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID beyond recording the feedback.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara reflected because she asked why her work fell short and planned specific changes, not because she recorded the feedback accurately or wrote more.
